author: tcoratger
content: This channel is dedicated to Ethereum's consensus layer transition to post-quantum cryptography.

author: tcoratger
content: There are several important topics we need to discuss here, along with some useful links:

author: tcoratger
content: - XMSS signature scheme: The specification can be found here: https://github.com/ethereum/EthLib/tree/master/EthLib/Cryptography/Xmss

author: tcoratger
content: - Validator public key registration with XMSS: We currently have two EIPs proposing different approaches: https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/pull/12609 and https://github.com/ethereum/EIPs/blob/master/EIPS/eip-8450.md

author: tcoratger
content: - Transition from BLS to XMSS: https://github.com/jtraglia/EIPs/pull/1 as <@592004585506340885> just shared.

author: tcoratger
content: - XMSS signature aggregation via SNARKs: The underlying machinery can be found here: https://github.com/leanEthereum/leanVM

author: tcoratger
content: - Networking: Post-quantum cryptographic objects are significantly larger than their elliptic-curve counterparts, which introduces new challenges for network communication and data propagation. Work is currently underway, with ongoing discussions and simulations.

author: tcoratger
content: It is important to note here that some of the elements specified above remain a work in progress. For instance, regarding the XMSS signature scheme, keccak is currently our strongest candidate for a hash function; however, discussions among researchers are still ongoing to ensure the right choice is made, as these decisions could shape Ethereum for decades to come.

author: potuz
content:
Hello, I have a question regarding leanVM aggregation for XMSS signatures. When aggregating BLS, the aggregator can cheaply keep the most current aggregate up to now, and when the validator client requests the aggregate to sign and broadcast, the beacon doesn't need to do any work, it just returns the current aggregate. This is a property of EC aggregation: a sum is pretty cheap and is associative. 

For XMSS it looks to me that this property is lost, is this correct? that is, I imagine that aggregators will need to be smart at which time they start aggregating? if you start too early your aggregate will be useless and if you start too late your aggregate will also be useless as most of the coverage will already be included in previous aggregates. Also this could make the recursion step also worse since you may be aggregating aggregates with very little marginal gain. 

I just want to get confirmation of the above statements from the PQ crowd cause depending on the answer to these issues we would have to specify very different strategies for the validator.md file on the fork. cc <@363800010518822915> <@592004585506340885>

author: tcoratger
content:
It is possible to merge aggregates from leanXMSS within leanVM, much like one would with BLS; however, while BLS—thanks to pairing properties—is extremely fast, the process for aggregating leanXMSS via leanVM is significantly slower (think seconds rather than microseconds).

- In BLS, an aggregate is a sum of points; adding a signature is essentially cost-free.
- With leanXMSS, an aggregate is a SNARK proof; updating it requires re-running the proof generation process.

Currently, the setup in leanVM is as follows:
- An aggregation step can accept up to 16 prior aggregates (child aggregates) as well as raw signatures.
- It outputs the union of the signers; if a signer appears twice, they are included and counted only once.
- The aggregator can maintain a running aggregate and continuously fold new data into it: `acc ← aggregate([acc], new_signatures)`. Given that prover time must be factored in, an aggregate produced at time T contains signatures received up to approximately time T minus the duration required for proof generation.

Additionally, a proof is roughly 250–350 KiB in size, compared to 96 bytes for BLS.

author: kevaundray
content:
Yeah this is correct. One strategy is to aggregate every X second, where X is how long it takes to aggregate N signatures.

So for example, we can set X to 1 which makes N = 1024.  The validator would then aggregate 1024 signatures every second (assuming they have received that many)

author: potuz
content:
The number 8 came from Electra. It was deemed that 8 different heads was good enough to make the chain finalized even when 88% of the blocks were missing. 

The thing is that with BLS aggregation, all attestations for the same head go in the same aggregate, the proposer does the final aggregation and there's never a need to include more than 8 heads. With XMSS, we can easily get more than 8 heads, or 16 or 64 for that matter. The attacker can force aggregates to include his own attestation for old blocks creating aggregates that can't be included unless we increase the number of heads allowed in a block. If we do increase the number of attestations allowed in a block then the top size explodes... but that analysis needs to be redone given that the STARK is 300KB

author: tcoratger
content:
Understood, then let me clarify a bit. Indeed, with BLS, one aggregate can only hold one message, so the number of heads in a block is the number of aggregates, I guess this is why we have the 8 stuff you describe.

leanVM works differently on two points.

**1. One proof can cover several heads.**
A proof attests to a set of `(pubkey, message)` pairs, with any messages. So, a block can carry one proof whether it covers 1 head or 64. Then, an extra head adds its message and its signer list, not another ~300 KB proof.

**2. Unwanted heads can be filtered out.**
Each aggregation step takes earlier aggregates as inputs, plus an explicit list of the pairs to publish (`declare`, see this line https://github.com/leanEthereum/leanVM/blob/64f80302521d8d51a2de03c7f257855b084f57bd/crates/rec_aggregation/src/aggregation/node.rs#L55). The pairs left out are still checked inside the proof, but they are not published. The aggregator re-proves at every step anyway, so filtering costs nothing extra.

To give an example:
- `P = aggregate(900 sigs on head H + 5 attacker sigs on old head V)` so that P covers H and V
- `P' = aggregate([P], declare = the 900 pairs on H) `so that P' covers H only

content: <@1257246783503994940> <@923866336382316594> have you guys looked at Justin's branch? I believe many of the comments above will be clarified when you look at that. We can wipe entirely clients and start fresh with a new spec. We can on the other hand try to keep a minimum fork that gets us to a PQ world. On blocks is simpler, which is the reason why a proof say for `{ heads {a,b,c},  committes { {list1}, {list2}, {list3}} , proof: STARK}` it will be encoded in the block as `attestations = {{ a, list1 }, {b, list2}, {c, list3}}, proof = STARK}`, that is, we keep the exact same attestation type we had before, and put the Stark outside the list.
